name: biogears-sbml-sepsis
title: BioGears sepsis core: engine vs SBML extraction

campaign_docs.name: BioGears sepsis core in Antimony: extraction report (Sauro)
campaign_docs.path: investigations/biogears-sbml-sepsis/sources/BioGears sepsis core in Antimony extraction report.pdf

lead:
BioGears is a lumped-parameter C++ whole-body physiology engine. Its sepsis
core — cardiovascular circuit, baroreflex, capillary fluid/albumin exchange,
and the McDaniel 2019 Acute Inflammatory Response — was extracted by Herbert
Sauro into a single Antimony model (91 state variables) that also exports to
SBML. That extraction was validated only against the paper's published
milestones, because the author could not run BioGears. This investigation runs
both: the real engine via viva-biogears and the SBML extraction via
viva-tellurium, side by side, to produce the run-for-run comparison the
extraction report could not.

at_a_glance.role: Parity gate — both sides hold the StandardMale baseline at rest, so later divergence is the model, not the starting state.
Agreement case — mild infection controlled on both sides; also the first sign of the engine's ambient fluctuation.

Headline — the full 9-observable severe comparison over 72 h: opposite decompensation mechanisms and a flipped milestone order (engine leads on SBP, extraction leads on MAP<65 shock; both cross the <65 threshold).
Runtime axis (composition engine) — the SBML composite is bit-identical under process-bigraph (Python) and viva-core (Rust); engine swap moves only framework overhead.
Synthesis — maps every divergence to the BioGears subsystem the extraction omits or simplifies.

Runtime axis (ODE integrator) — the sepsis ODE is stiff, so an explicit/Rust integrator (viva-hybrid-style) cannot speed it up; the speed levers are a better stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate.

biological_story:
Sepsis in BioGears is a race between an inflammatory response and the
cardiovascular system that keeps blood pressure up. A bacterial load seeds the
tissue; the Acute Inflammatory Response (McDaniel 2019) amplifies, tissue integrity
falls, capillaries leak, and fluid moves from blood to interstitium. The heart and
vasculature compensate — heart rate and vascular tone rise — until, in severe
sepsis, that compensation fatigues and pressure falls toward septic shock.

Herbert Sauro extracted this core from BioGears' C++ into a single 91-state Antimony
model. The inflammation half of the race he translated faithfully: run against the
real engine, tissue integrity and pathogen load track it almost bit-for-bit in both
mild and severe infection. The cardiovascular half is where the two implementations
part. BioGears carries a whole driven body — a nutrition schedule, temperature,
respiration, renal fluid handling, nitric-oxide and fever vasodilation, continuous
baroreflex control — so even a mild, controlled infection shows pressures wandering
over ~10 mmHg as the body eats, compensates and drifts. The extraction is an
autonomous ODE: it holds those inputs at baseline, so the same infection produces a
smooth, near-flat trace. Same clinical outcome, no ambient life.

Under severe sepsis the two push blood pressure down into shock by opposite
routes (over 72 h both cross the MAP<65 threshold — the engine to MAP 64 at 69 h,
the extraction to MAP 58 at 54 h). The real engine fails as a pump — cardiac output falls while vascular
tone holds — a hypodynamic, low-output decline. The extraction instead keeps
output up and gives up its vascular tone, swinging from vasoconstriction into
vasodilation (a warm, hyperdynamic pattern), because its one remaining vasomotor
pathway (the inflammation-driven
sympathetic arc) has to carry a response the engine spreads across nitric oxide,
fever vasodilation and renal fluid handling — pathways the extraction omits or
leaves inert. Strip those out and the model still gets sepsis right in outline, but
it gets the body's hemodynamic defence of blood pressure wrong in mechanism and on
a flipped timeline — ~11 hours late to systolic hypotension, yet ~15 hours early to
MAP<65 shock, because its one vasodilatory arc overshoots. That is the functional
difference between the two runtimes.
question:
Does the Antimony/SBML extraction of the BioGears sepsis core reproduce the
real BioGears engine run-for-run — not merely against the McDaniel et al. 2019
paper milestones — and where does it diverge, and why?
hypothesis:
The extraction reproduces BioGears' healthy baseline and the qualitative mild
and severe infection outcomes, but the severe course lags the engine by several
hours and the two diverge on observables fed by processes the extraction does
not translate (urine, fever-driven vasodilation, lactate, intracellular water).

executive.what_is_this:
A side-by-side comparison of the BioGears sepsis core run two ways — the real
BioGears 8.2.0 engine (viva-biogears) versus its SBML/Antimony extraction
(viva-tellurium) — across a healthy baseline and mild and severe infection,
plus two runtime axes: one comparing the Python process-bigraph engine with the
Rust viva-core engine on the same composite (the composition engine), and one
asking whether a faster or compiled ODE integrator could speed up the SBML model
(the numerical solver).
executive.verdict:
The extraction's inflammation core is bit-identical to the engine, and ALL
divergence lives in the hemodynamic layer. Run-for-run (mild 48 h, severe
extended to 72 h): baseline parity holds; mild stays controlled on both sides;
at the severe horizon tissue integrity (0.243/0.243) and pathogen load
(330.2/330.6) match to ~0.1% in every arm. But the hemodynamics diverge two ways.
(1) Even at mild infection the engine fluctuates continuously (SBP range ~11 mmHg,
from its nutrition schedule and full homeostatic control) while the autonomous
extraction sits within ~0.6 mmHg. (2) Under severe sepsis both arms cross into
MAP<65 shock by OPPOSITE mechanisms and in FLIPPED order — the engine by a
hypodynamic, low-output route (cardiac output 5.8 → 4.0 L/min, SVR ~flat, MAP<65
at 69.3 h) while the extraction by a hyperdynamic, vasodilatory route (SVR swings
0.93 → 1.13 → 0.60, cardiac output rebounds to 5.5, MAP<65 at 54.1 h). The
extraction lags the engine by ~11 h on systolic pressure (SBP<100 at 37.5 h vs
26.6 h) yet reaches the MAP<65 shock threshold ~15 h EARLIER, because its deeper
SVR vasodilation drags MAP = CO·SVR down first. Both the mechanism split and the
flipped timing trace to the vasomotor/fluid/metabolic subsystems
the extraction omits (inert nitric oxide, absent fever vasodilation, no renal
fluid handling, no lactate, no intracellular water). This is the engine-vs-
extraction comparison the report could not make.
executive.verdict_detail:
All four arms ran (severity 1 & 3 × engine & SBML, locally-built BioGears
8.2.0; mild to 48 h, severe extended to 72 h), plus a synthesis study (05) that
maps every divergence to a specific BioGears subsystem. Parity gate closed;
cross-engine runtime axis bit-identical. The extraction is a faithful surrogate
for the inflammation core and for qualitative outcomes, but it is NOT a drop-in
replacement for BioGears' cardiovascular dynamics: it misses the engine's ambient
physiological variation and reaches MAP<65 shock by a different hemodynamic route
and in flipped order — both arms cross the <65 threshold within 72 h (extraction
at 54.1 h, engine at 69.3 h), the extraction ~15 h ahead despite lagging ~11 h on
systolic pressure.

On performance (study 06), the SBML route is not a shortcut to speed by way of a
faster integrator. The sepsis ODE is stiff, so the one solver class that works is
an implicit stiff method (CVODE/BDF) — already compiled C inside libroadrunner.
An explicit fixed-step integrator (the kind our viva-hybrid Rust engine uses) is
unstable on the real model and gets the fast cardiovascular states wrong by more
than 100x even at 173 million steps per 48 h run. An independent viva-hybrid trial
shows that even where explicit integration is valid, a from-scratch Rust
integrator beats compiled numba by only ~2x. The real speed levers are a better or
warm-started stiff solver, GPU parallelism across many virtual patients, or a
reduced-order surrogate — not reimplementing the integrator in another language.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
The SBML extraction faithfully reproduces the BioGears sepsis core's inflammation
(bit-identical) and its qualitative outcomes, but it is not a drop-in replacement
for the engine's cardiovascular behaviour: it lacks the engine's ambient
physiological fluctuation, and under severe sepsis it reaches MAP<65 shock by a
different hemodynamic mechanism and on a flipped timeline (lagging ~11 h on
systolic pressure but reaching MAP<65 shock ~15 h earlier) — divergences that map
cleanly onto the vasomotor, fluid and metabolic subsystems the extraction omits.
evidence_for: Inflammation states (tissue integrity, blood pathogen) agree to <0.1% in both arms (study 05 heatmap).
SBML baseline matches BioGears StandardMale targets within tolerance (study 01).
Mild infection controlled on both sides with no hypotension (study 02).
evidence_against: Severe decompensation mechanism differs: engine hypodynamic (CO-failure), extraction hyperdynamic (vasodilatory) — 38% CO / 36% SVR peak divergence over 72 h (study 03/05); both arms cross the <65 shock threshold, the extraction ~15 h before the engine (MAP<65 at 54.1 h vs 69.3 h).
Severe hemodynamic milestones lag ~11 h (SBP<100 at 37.5 h vs 26.6 h; study 03).
Engine fluctuates continuously even at mild; the autonomous extraction is near-flat (study 02/05).
Omitted/inert subsystems — nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal/urine, lactate, intracellular water — are exactly the pathways that move the divergent observables (study 05).
caveats: 'Functional-difference' attributions (study 05) come from the extraction report's own 'Differences from BioGears' inventory; they are documented omissions, not newly-measured mechanisms.
viva-biogears runs its InfectionModerate nutrition schedule; the extraction models no meals — a documented scenario delta that accounts for much of the mild-arm fluctuation.
Single runs per severity (mild 48 h, severe 72 h); no multi-seed ensemble (the engine is deterministic for a fixed scenario).

The integrator benchmark (study 06) is run on a 60 s window with step counts extrapolated to 48 h, and uses roadrunner's own rk4/rk45/cvode integrators (rk4 is the same algorithm as the viva-hybrid Rust engine, not viva-hybrid itself); the ~2x Rust-vs-compiled figure is carried over from the viva-hybrid repo's non-stiff benchmark, not re-measured on the sepsis model.

competing_frameworks.name: Extraction validated against paper milestones only (status quo)
competing_frameworks.relation: This investigation supersedes it with a run-for-run engine comparison.

studies.name: 01-baseline-parity
studies.title: Baseline parity
studies.question:
At rest (no infection), do the real BioGears engine and the SBML/Antimony
extraction settle to the same StandardMale baseline haemodynamics, so that any
later divergence under infection is attributable to the model and not to a
mismatched starting state?

findings.summary: Engine and SBML baselines match at rest — run-for-run parity holds.
findings.detail:
Real BioGears 8.2.0 (severity 0, 5 min): SBP 114.87, DBP 74.54, HR 72.24,
CO 5.81 L/min. SBML extraction (severity 0, 30 s): SBP 114.6, DBP 73.48,
HR 71.5, CO 5.905 L/min. Max difference ~1 mmHg / ~0.7 bpm / ~0.1 L/min —
well within physiological tolerance. Both read uninfected (blood_pathogen ~0,
tissue_integrity ~1.0). The parity gate PASSES, so divergence under
infection (studies 02/03) reflects the model, not the starting state.

studies.claim:
Both sides hold the BioGears StandardMale baseline and match each other at rest:
real engine SBP 114.9 / DBP 74.5 / HR 72.2 / CO 5.81 L/min vs SBML extraction
SBP 114.6 / DBP 73.5 / HR 71.5 / CO 5.9 L/min — all within physiological
tolerance. The run-for-run parity gate PASSES; infection divergence measured in
studies 02/03 is attributable to the model, not a mismatched starting state.

derived.insight: Engine and SBML baselines match at rest — run-for-run parity holds.

studies.name: 02-mild-infection
studies.title: Mild infection (severity 1)
studies.question:
Under a mild infection (severity 1), does the SBML extraction reproduce the
BioGears engine's course — a controlled infection that resolves without
progressing to hypotension — run for run?

findings.summary: Mild infection stays controlled on both sides; no hypotension milestones crossed.
findings.detail:
Both arms, severity 1, 48 h, infection at t=0: SBP<100, MAP<65 and HR>90 are
never reached (sustained) on either side. tissue_integrity minimum
0.96755/0.96755; peak blood_pathogen 6.2983/6.2983 — near-identical.
Hemodynamics differ over the course (SBP max-abs ~10.6 mmHg, DBP ~5, MAP ~7.6,
HR ~6.3 bpm, blood_volume ~0.57 L, plus a cardiac-output offset), but the qualitative mild outcome agrees run-for-run.

studies.claim:
Under mild infection both the real engine and the SBML extraction keep the
infection controlled over 48 h — neither crosses into hypotension (no SBP<100,
no MAP<65, no HR>90) — and the inflammation core matches almost exactly
(tissue integrity min 0.9676/0.9676, peak pathogen 6.298/6.298). Mild is the
agreement case that frames the severe-arm divergence.

derived.insight: Mild infection stays controlled on both sides; no hypotension milestones crossed.

studies.name: 03-severe-infection
studies.title: Severe infection (severity 3)
studies.question:
Under a severe infection (severity 3), does the SBML extraction track the
BioGears engine's collapse sequence run-for-run, and how large is the known
timing divergence (the extraction report saw the severe course lag by ~8-10 h
against the paper)?

findings.summary: Over 72 h both arms cross into MAP<65 shock, but the milestone order flips: engine leads on SBP (−11 h), extraction leads on MAP (−15 h).
findings.detail:
Both arms, severity 3, 72 h, infection at t=0, run-for-run:
- SBP < 100 mmHg: engine 26.55 h, extraction 37.47 h -> extraction +10.9 h LATE.
- HR > 90 /min:  engine 26.77 h, extraction 37.55 h -> extraction +10.8 h LATE.
- MAP < 65 mmHg: engine 69.33 h, extraction 54.07 h -> extraction 15.3 h EARLY.
- SVR ratio minimum: engine 0.949 (barely dips), extraction 0.646 — the
  extraction over-shoots the vasodilation.
The flip is mechanistic: the engine's cold, low-output decline (CO falls,
SVR ~flat) drops systolic pressure early but holds MAP up longer, while the
extraction's deep SVR vasodilation collapses MAP (= CO·SVR) first even though
its SBP lags. The systolic lag most likely comes from processes the extraction
does not translate (urine loss, fever-driven skin vasodilation, lactate,
intracellular water); the early MAP crossing comes from its un-tempered
vasodilatory arc.

findings.summary: The inflammation / pathogen core matches the engine almost bit-for-bit.
findings.detail:
tissue_integrity minimum 0.2431 (engine) vs 0.2430 (extraction); peak
blood_pathogen 330.2 vs 330.6 at the 72 h horizon (neither course has fully
resolved — resolved = false on both arms). The Acute Inflammatory Response the
extraction copied from BioGears reproduces the engine's dynamics to ~1e-4 for
tissue integrity (~1e-3 relative on peak pathogen); divergence is confined to
the hemodynamic response, not the inflammation model.

findings.summary: In CO–SVR phase space the two arms are orthogonal: MAP = 17.34·CO·SVR holds in both, so each reaches MAP<65 shock by a different axis.
findings.detail:
MAP decomposes as MAP = k·CO·SVR with k = 17.34 mmHg·min·mL/(L·s), a
relation that holds to <0.5% (CV 0.26% engine, 0.45% extraction) with the
SAME constant in both arms — so the two trajectories live in one CO–SVR
plane and the divergence is purely which axis each moves along. From the
shared baseline (CO ~5.8 L/min, SVR ~0.95) the engine slides along the CO
axis (5.78 → 3.99 L/min, SVR ~flat 0.95) to MAP 64 — a cold, low-output
decline — while the extraction slides along the SVR axis (CO holds/rebounds
4.56 → 5.5, SVR swings 0.93 → 1.13 → 0.60) to MAP 58 — a warm, vasodilatory
decline. Both now cross the MAP<65 shock threshold (engine at 69.3 h, MAP end
64.0; extraction at 54.1 h, MAP end 58.1), by orthogonal mechanisms; this is
the geometric statement of the vasomotor overshoot characterized in study 05.
See charts/05_severe_phase_portrait_co_svr.svg.

studies.claim:
Run-for-run over 72 h, the SBML extraction reproduces BioGears' severe-sepsis
inflammation almost exactly (tissue integrity 0.243/0.243, peak pathogen
330.2/330.6) while its hemodynamic collapse diverges in BOTH timing and
mechanism. On the systolic milestone the extraction LAGS: SBP crosses 100 mmHg
at 37.5 h vs 26.6 h in the engine (a 10.9 h lag), with the same ~11 h lag on the
HR>90 compensation. But on mean arterial pressure the order FLIPS — the
extraction reaches the MAP<65 shock threshold FIRST, at 54.1 h vs the engine's
69.3 h (15.3 h earlier), because its deeper SVR vasodilation (ratio min 0.65 vs
the engine's ~flat 0.95) drags MAP = CO·SVR down faster. Both arms now cross into
sustained hypotensive shock within 72 h (MAP ends 58 mmHg extraction, 64 mmHg
engine); neither course fully resolves. This is the engine-vs-extraction
comparison the extraction report could not make.

derived.insight: Over 72 h both arms cross into MAP<65 shock, but the milestone order flips: engine leads on SBP (−11 h), extraction leads on MAP (−15 h).

studies.name: 04-engine-runtime
studies.title: Engine runtime + cross-engine determinism
studies.question:
Does running the SBML sepsis composite on the Rust viva-core engine instead of
the Python process-bigraph engine produce the same results, and how do their
wall-clock times compare on this real physiology workload?

findings.summary: viva-core drives the real Tellurium process and matches process-bigraph bit-identically.
findings.detail:
viva_core.run drives the real TelluriumProcess via a thin adapter
(viva_simulation_core/analysis/vc_adapter.py) that works around current
viva-core MVP limits (stock address, core injection, empty containers,
map-store overwrites) WITHOUT changing the roadrunner computation. On warm
runs the final state is bit-identical to process-bigraph across all 9
observables (max abs diff 0.0). A fresh-process first roadrunner run differs
by ~1e-6 relative (a Python-side cold-start effect), so the cold tolerance
is rtol=1e-5.

findings.summary: Wall-clock is framework overhead, not a speedup, for this single-heavy-process composite.
findings.detail:
severity 0, 10 s interval, one measurement each (600 s / 3600 s are
simulated time): 600 s -> process-bigraph 25.3 s, viva-core 25.9 s;
3600 s -> process-bigraph 139.9 s, viva-core 125.8 s. Essentially equal, as
predicted: the libroadrunner solver dominates and the tick loop is a small
slice. These single measurements are indicative, not benchmarked.

findings.summary: The SBML extraction runs a matched 48 h sim modestly faster than the real engine (1.2-1.6x), not orders of magnitude.
findings.detail:
Committed wall-clock (meta.wall_s) for one matched 48 h simulation: mild —
real BioGears engine 3.35 h vs SBML extraction 2.15 h (1.56x); severe — engine
3.38 h vs SBML 2.81 h (1.20x). The extraction is modestly faster, not an order
of magnitude, because integrating the stiff 91-state ODE in roadrunner is
itself heavy (study 06). This is the model-vs-model axis relevant to large
virtual-patient sweeps — distinct from the composition-engine swap above
(process-bigraph vs viva-core), which is bit-identical and overhead-only.

studies.claim:
viva-core drives the real Tellurium/roadrunner process and reproduces
process-bigraph bit-identically (max abs diff 0.0 across all 9 observables on
warm runs). Wall-clock is essentially equal — a single heavy process means the
engine swap measures framework overhead, not solver time (no ~160x here).

derived.insight: viva-core drives the real Tellurium process and matches process-bigraph bit-identically.

studies.name: 05-divergence-mechanism
studies.title: Divergence mechanism: engine vs extraction functionality
studies.question:
Across all nine observables and both infection severities, WHERE does the SBML
extraction diverge from the BioGears engine, and WHICH BioGears functionality —
translated, simplified, or omitted — accounts for each divergence? This is the
synthesis study: it turns the run-for-run comparison into a map of the functional
differences between the two implementations.

findings.summary: The inflammation core is bit-identical; all divergence is hemodynamic.
findings.detail:
Peak relative divergence: tissue integrity 0.0% (both arms) and blood pathogen
0.0% / 0.1% (mild / severe). The hemodynamic observables carry everything —
mild 4.5–9.7%, severe up to 38.2% (cardiac output) and 35.9% (SVR) over the
72 h horizon. The 21-state AIR module reproduces the engine to ~1e-4; the
divergence is a property of the cardiovascular/fluid layer, not the
inflammation model.

findings.summary: Under severe sepsis both arms reach MAP<65 shock by opposite mechanisms, and the milestone order flips.
findings.detail:
Engine: cardiac output falls 5.78 → 3.99 L/min while SVR stays ~flat
(0.954 → 0.929) — a hypodynamic, low-output pattern; MAP crosses 65 at 69.3 h
(ends 64). Extraction: SVR vasoconstricts to 1.13 (compensation) then falls to
0.60 (sympathetic fatigue) while cardiac output rebounds to 5.5 — a
hyperdynamic, warm pattern; MAP crosses 65 at 54.1 h (ends 58). Both reach
sustained hypotensive shock, different route (MAP ≈ CO × SVR), and the order
flips: the extraction lags on SBP<100 (+11 h) but leads on MAP<65 (−15 h)
because its deeper SVR vasodilation pulls MAP down first. The extraction's
single AIR→sympathetic vasomotor arc overshoots; the engine's full
cardiovascular control, with the omitted vasodilatory pathways, stays muted.

findings.summary: Even at mild infection the engine fluctuates continuously; the extraction idles.
findings.detail:
Mild arm, matched outcome: engine SBP ranges ~11 mmHg with continuous
meal/baroreflex fluctuation (its InfectionModerate nutrition schedule plus full
homeostatic control), while the autonomous SBML extraction holds within
~0.6 mmHg. The engine is an open, driven whole-body system; the extraction is a
closed ODE at equilibrium perturbed only by the infection — same clinical
outcome, none of the ambient physiological dynamics.

findings.summary: Every divergence maps to a documented omitted or simplified BioGears subsystem.
findings.detail:
From the extraction report's "Differences from BioGears": nitric oxide is inert
in the code (paper describes a vasodilatory effect), fever-driven skin
vasodilation is absent (temperature not translated), the renal module is off
(no urine output), lactate and intracellular-water shifts are not translated,
respiration/chemoreceptors are held at baseline, and no nutrition inputs are
modelled. These are exactly the vasomotor, fluid and metabolic pathways that
couple into SVR, cardiac output and blood volume — the observables that diverge.
See 03_functional_difference_matrix.

studies.claim:
The inflammation core is bit-identical between the two implementations (tissue
integrity diverges <0.02% and blood pathogen ~0.1% in both arms), so ALL
divergence lives in the hemodynamic layer. Two functional differences explain it.
(1) Ambient dynamics: even under mild infection, where outcomes agree, the
engine's pressures fluctuate over an ~11 mmHg range (its nutrition schedule plus
full homeostatic control) while the autonomous extraction — a closed ODE with no
meal, respiration or temperature inputs — sits within ~0.6 mmHg. (2) Decompensation
mechanism: over 72 h both arms cross the MAP<65 shock threshold (engine at 69.3 h
to MAP 64, extraction at 54.1 h to MAP 58) but by opposite routes — the engine
declines hypodynamically (cardiac output 5.8 → 4.0 L/min, SVR ~flat at 0.95) while
the extraction declines hyperdynamically (SVR 0.93 → 1.13 → 0.60, cardiac output
rebounding to 5.5). Over the longer horizon the gap widens to peak divergence 38%
on cardiac output and 36% on SVR, and the milestone order flips: the extraction
lags the engine by ~11 h on SBP<100 yet leads it by ~15 h on MAP<65, because its
single AIR→sympathetic arc overshoots the vasomotor swing that the engine's omitted
pathways (inert nitric oxide, absent fever vasodilation, no renal fluid handling,
no lactate) would otherwise temper.

derived.insight: The inflammation core is bit-identical; all divergence is hemodynamic.

studies.name: 06-ode-integrator-runtime
studies.title: ODE integrator runtime: can a Rust/compiled solver speed up the SBML model?
studies.question:
The SBML extraction is attractive partly as a potentially faster route than the
full BioGears C++ engine. Would reimplementing its ODE *integrator* — for example
in Rust, the way our viva-hybrid engine does with a fixed-step RK4 — make the
SBML sepsis model meaningfully faster than the libroadrunner (CVODE) path we
already use? This study separates the two different "engines" people mean: study
04 swapped the *composition* engine (Python process-bigraph vs Rust viva-core);
this study is about the *numerical ODE integrator* that actually advances the
91 states.

findings.summary: The sepsis ODE is stiff; explicit fixed-step RK4 (viva-hybrid's integrator) is unstable.
findings.detail:
On the real 91-state model over a 60 s window, roadrunner's rk4 (fixed-step,
the same algorithm as the viva-hybrid Rust engine) diverges to non-finite
values for every step dt >= 0.05 s. Remaining finite requires dt <= 0.02 s,
which is 8.6 million steps for a single 48 h simulation. This is the textbook
stiffness signature: the fast cardiovascular modes force the explicit step far
below what accuracy alone would need.

findings.summary: Even at 173 M steps per 48 h, the fast cardiovascular states are still wrong.
findings.detail:
At dt = 0.001 s (172.8 million RK4 steps for one 48 h run), explicit RK4
converges to the wrong trajectory on the cardiovascular subsystem: vena-cava
pressure 406 vs the true 1.58, cardiac-cycle timer 60 vs 0.39, aortic pressure
1000 vs 38, right-ventricular volume 327 vs 18. 30 of 91 states are off by
>1% and 5 by >100%, all of them hemodynamic, while the slow inflammation and
metabolic states track (median error 0.3%). The error is dt-independent from
dt = 0.02 s down to 0.001 s, so this is a wrong trajectory, not unconverged
step size. The stiffness lives in the cardiovascular loop — the same subsystem
where the engine and extraction diverge (studies 03, 05).

findings.summary: The adaptive explicit solver is stability-limited; the stiff solver is already compiled C.
findings.detail:
rk45 (adaptive explicit Dormand-Prince) is stability-limited on this model and
could not finish the 60 s window within a 45 s cap, while cvode (stiff BDF)
integrated it in seconds. The solver that works — CVODE — is already compiled C
(SUNDIALS) inside libroadrunner. A reimplementation in Rust would be rewriting
already-native numerics, not removing interpreter overhead.

findings.summary: Independent viva-hybrid trial: a Rust integrator beats compiled numba by only ~2x.
findings.detail:
The viva-hybrid repo ran exactly the "define the model abstractly, compile the
integrator to Rust" experiment on a non-stiff bursting-gene benchmark — the
favorable case, where explicit integration is valid. Result (its
docs/results/trial-report.md): 46x faster than plain Python but only 2.01x vs a
numba-jitted baseline — MARGINAL, on a >=5x go / <2x dead line. Against
already-compiled numerics a Rust rewrite buys ~2x, not an order of magnitude.
This is the second, independent leg of the conclusion: neither the stiff case
(wrong tool) nor the non-stiff case (marginal) makes the integrator the speed
lever.

studies.claim:
The sepsis ODE is stiff, and that settles the question. An explicit fixed-step
RK4 — viva-hybrid's integrator — is numerically unstable on the real model: it
diverges to non-finite values for every step dt >= 0.05 s. At steps fine enough
to stay finite, it converges to the *wrong* trajectory: even at dt = 0.001 s
(172.8 million steps for a single 48 h simulation) the fast cardiovascular states
are wrong by more than 100x (vena-cava pressure 406 vs the true 1.58; aortic
pressure 1000 vs 38; 30 of 91 states off by >1%, 5 by >100%), while the slow
inflammation and metabolic states track (median error 0.3%). The adaptive
explicit method (rk45) is stability-limited to steps so small it could not finish
a 60 s window in 45 s. The one solver that works — a stiff BDF method (CVODE) — is
already compiled C (SUNDIALS) inside libroadrunner and integrates the window in
seconds. The stiffness lives in the cardiovascular loop, which is exactly the
subsystem where the engine and the extraction diverge (studies 03, 05). An
independent trial (the viva-hybrid repo) shows that even on a *non-stiff* model,
where explicit integration is valid, a from-scratch Rust engine beat compiled
numba by only ~2.0x. So reimplementing the integrator is not an order-of-magnitude
speed lever for this model. The real ODE-speed levers are a better or warm-started
stiff solver, GPU parallelism across many virtual patients, or a reduced-order
surrogate.

derived.insight: The sepsis ODE is stiff; explicit fixed-step RK4 (viva-hybrid's integrator) is unstable.
